analysis.one_liner: Phases out the federal estate and gift tax over ten years, repealing it entirely by 2009.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have eliminated the estate tax that applies only to the largest inheritances, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut estate and gift tax rates by five percentage points each year starting in 1999, wiping out the tax entirely for deaths and gifts after 2008. Estate tax rates ran up to 55% under then-current law. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 1998 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The federal estate tax only applies above a filing threshold, so repeal is worth the most to families passing on multi-million-dollar farms, businesses, and investment portfolios. Gift-tax repeal also benefits wealthy families transferring money during life.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces estate and gift tax rates by five percentage points each year from 1999 through 2008, reaching full repeal for estates of decedents dying and gifts made after December 31, 2008.

The bill's stated rationale is that estate tax rates of up to 55% exceed rates on ordinary income and capital gains, making the tax, in the sponsors' words, 'confiscatory' for family businesses and heirs.
Also reduces the credit for state death taxes over the same ten-year schedule, coordinating the phaseout with state-level inheritance taxes.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately other taxpayers — loses the revenue the estate tax raises, which falls entirely on the largest estates. Because the bill also shrinks the federal credit for state death taxes, state governments collect less inheritance tax revenue as well.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state treasuries, and other taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The estate tax is one of the few federal taxes paid exclusively by the wealthiest estates; repealing it shrinks federal revenue while leaving the benefit concentrated among the largest inheritances, since smaller estates never owed the tax in the first place.
The bill simultaneously reduces the federal credit for state death taxes, cutting the inheritance tax revenue state governments collect over the same ten years.
The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so the full cost of repeal would add to the deficit or require higher taxes elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to heirs of the largest estates, since the estate tax only applies above a threshold and reaches a small share of deaths. The cost — lost federal revenue and reduced state inheritance-tax collections — is spread across everyone else. As drafted, the bill had no revenue offsets.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in July 1998 and sat there until the Congress ended that January, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Nighthorse Campbell introduced the bill on July 16, 1998, with four Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The bill received no further action of any kind before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal and state treasuries kept the estate and inheritance tax revenue, and no one else gained. The wealthiest estates did not get the repeal their sponsors sought, but the bill had so little momentum that nothing was at risk of changing.

for.name: Sen. Ben Nighthorse Campbell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after its referral in July 1998.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; there were no votes, so the broader partisan split never got measured.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and their estates' planners
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the estate tax, which applies only above a threshold and is owed almost exclusively by the largest estates. It died, so the tax — and the estate-planning industry built around it — stayed in place.
The bill would have reduced the federal credit for state death taxes, shrinking state inheritance-tax collections over ten years. State treasuries are better off that it failed.
